newsitem.title: USA: NY palladium, platinum end up for third day.
newsitem.headline: NY palladium, platinum end up for third day.

text.p: COMEX gold and silver futures ended lower Wednesday, but NYMEX platinum and palladium rose for the third session in a row, as the disruption to Russian supplies again began to be felt, traders said.

"The platinum metals group looks good fundamentally, and potentially there's a huge move up ahead which may spill over into gold and silver, as the platinum/gold spread widens, but it may not, as the link to gold is not strong fundamentally," said, Scott Meyers, an analyst with Pioneer Futures in New York.
NYMEX June palladium ended up $5.75 an ounce at $159.50, its highest level since early March, after spot palladium fixed at $157.75 in London Wednesday morning, the highest level in 21 months.
The NYMEX June/September spread went into a rare backwardation around $1.50 an ounce Wednesday, from a contango around $1.00 an ounce earlier this month.
NYMEX July platinum ended up $3.30 an ounce at $373.00 an ounce, while the October NYMEX platinum/COMEX gold spread widened to $19.30 an ounce from a two month low around $10.20 on Monday.

In the absence of Russian supplies for four months now, some owners of palladium stockpiled in Switzerland were moving to take delivery, but the Swiss holders had lent out some of the metal, forcing them to borrow the metal to make deliveries, platinum group metals traders said.
In the spot market palladium lease rates soared to around 16 percent as a result Wednesday, platinum group metals traders said.

"With Russian supplies drying up, fabricators are increasingly dependent on world stockpiles which probably amount to a few months worth of consumption," CRU International analyst Tony Warwick-Ching said.
"Swiss exports of palladium to the U.S. jumped in January and some of this may be being onshipped to Japan," he said.

Earlier this week a Russian trade official in Tokyo said there would be no shipments of Russian palladium to Japan in April and possibly none in May, while Russian exports would be much lower overall in 1997.
Talks on the Russian/Japanese supply contract broke down last December due to Russian fiscal and administrative problems.
Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and Japan accounts for about 40 percent of demand for use in automotive and electronic applications.
"The Russians look like they are getting down to a critical level in their palladium stockpiles and may be adopting a deliberate strategy of lowering their exports," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.
Meanwhile, COMEX June gold ended down 80 cents at $350.50 an ounce, but is still seen trapped in its $348.30-358.00 range of the past month.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $347.80/30 compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $347.80 and the New York close Tuesday around $348.30/80.
COMEX May silver closed down 0.5 cent at $4.775 an ounce, though the contract has recovered this week from a contract low at $4.655 seen last Thursday.
The expiry of May gold, silver and platinum options on Friday this week is unlikely to provide much direction, traders said, as open interest is low.

May is not an active month for COMEX gold or NYMEX platinum and even in the more active May silver futures and options, open interest in calls and puts is concentrated at strike prices well above current futures prices.
